data.name: Cantata
data.detailed_description:
A rebellion has broken out disrupting the military force controlling the galaxy titled the 111th Reign of Humanity and Prosper, a swarm of robots calling themselves the “Unified Spirit” have risen up against the shackles of their human masters with the dream of a better world. The final stand is taking place on the unexplored planet of Shoal, where legends, Gods and creatures of the shadows meet reality… unknown to humans or robots, the planet itself has awoken - and its people are fighting to save it.

Play as a Commanding Officer for each faction as you work your way through the campaign to uncover the planet, crush the rebellion or to create a better world. Manage your resources, troops and capture regions across the planet's surface. Be careful of your choices, it is not only the enemy forces you must watch out for but the treacherous planet itself.

EXPLORE AN ALIEN PLANET

Cantata takes you to a far off planet filled with vibrant colours, striking characters and a unique soundtrack that seems to echo through the galaxy. Each chapter of the campaign plays through as unique stand alone stories allowing you to uncover the history of each faction. Each map holds secrets for players to uncover which can aid you across the campaign - you’ll need to do effective recon to determine the best approach in battle. Beware though, the planet of Shoal isn't one to let you idly move across its surface. Just like any other faction, the planet itself takes a turn every round, giving it the ability to fight back against the war on its surface with weather, fauna, and other mysteries.

A GENRE DEFINING GAME

Combining elements from Grand Strategy titles with the small-scale skirmishes of classic Tactics games, in Cantata you’ll start with a small base of operations and crucial few units, and then bring your grand strategic vision to life by building new structures, managing your regions, and expanding your army. As your presence on the planet Shoal grows you’ll be keeping a close eye on not only the empire you’ve built but also growing threats across the map.


MAKE THE GAME YOUR OWN

Every single campaign map has been made with the exact same tool you’ll have access to in game. You have the full suite of options in your hands to make amazing tactical strategy maps. And if you get bored of our units, you can import your own custom units and terrains and make your own fully custom maps to share with everyone else in Steam Workshop. From small-sided skirmishes to epic, planet-sized conflicts, what kind of story do you want to create?

PLAY TOGETHER WITH FRIENDS

With both local and online multiplayer you can challenge friends and strangers across scenarios hand made using our modding tools or in our existing maps. Claim regions, out-manoeuvre your enemies, and surprise them with your unexpected ambushes. Cut off their supply lines, or meet them head-on at the front of battle. The choice is yours.

data.short_description: Crash-landed in the universe of Cantata, will you expand your empire or bring peace to the war torn planet? Grow your army, manage resources and discover the colourful planet of Shoal, its people, and the armed forces overrunning this land in this genre-defining Grand Tactics game.

reviews.review:
I'd been following [i]Cantata[/i] since around Covid. It looked like everything I wanted a mainstream strategy game to be - innovative, strategically diverse, beautiful, compellingly written...

I remember an interview close to release, where one of the developers threw out confidently 'there's no stopping [i]Cantata[/i]!'

Then came the release, and with it came the mixed reviews and I took note.
Looked like a mess, however beautiful it might be. 
Turned out, there in fact was a lot of stuff stopping [i]Cantata[/i].

Now I took a lesson from that.

[h1]ALWAYS TRUST YOUR GUT AND NEVER TRUST THE F@CKING REVIEWS[/h1]

What happens when a truly unique game comes out? 
No, it doesn't get recognised. 
No, it doesn't get praise.

It gets buried under an orgy of 'this guame isin't like that gayme me know hou to pley, me must learn nyuw skills, me [i]consumer[/i] sensebylytyies be ofendid!'

Somehow - I don't f@cking know how - the developers managed to mingle real-time strategy dynamics with those of a turn-based one. I realise [i]Advance Wars[/i] was sort of an inspiration, but this goes so far above and beyond.

With three [i]absolutely, completely, radically[/i] different factions - that have [i]absolutely, completely, radically[/i] different economies and [i]absolutely, completely, radically[/i] different means of transportation around the huge game maps - this Aztec codex looking interactive mural with late 70s  synth soundtrack is ideal mainstream strategy material.

You will always have to keep your troops supplied by growing your economy and capturing new regions, so whenever you go out conquering, you must build infrastructure.

Humans have traditional industry.
Aliens harness the great circle of life letting their healer collect resources and have the option of reincarnating spirits of fallen warriors.
Machines plain scrap anything that breaks and refashion it into their backbone.

Ammo is produced and physically put into your unit inventory (they all have one).

Everything is a resource. Both strategic (a fallen warrior shadow needs to get to the choppa to fight another day) and tactical (that corpse blocks an enemy shooter from getting into position to finish my valuable but momentarily low-health unit).
And every one of the resources can be contextually used differently for different purposes.

Terrain impacts unit speed. 
And, like I said, units of different factions get different means of transportation. 
Some have vehicles, others - teleporters.
And you must develop your infrastructure accordingly.

As your units gain experience, they learn to perform stronger attacks to spend global resources on. Occasionally it leads to just a few of your units cutting out a path in a horde of enemies.

You are not limited to one strategy for any given faction either. 
Say, as aliens do you go in melee as the hunters or do you turn on horde mode and play [i]Cabela: Big Game Hinter[/i] with that outpost, sicking a cheap and replaceable summonable mammoth avalanche onto them?

And now for the best part.
It's 
All
Free
Form.

A huge map where you plan your offensives however you wish, and then do your best to execute them without ruining the economy. 
I cannot begin to describe how satisfying it is to put together a successful offensive, where every tile of movement and weapon range begins to matter and you are constantly counting your resources and planning individual resupply runs. 
It is immensely, immensely rewarding, and a feeling I only ever really had in something like [url=https://steamcommunity.com/profiles/76561198081477001/recommended/63900?snr=1_5_9__402]Fantasy Wars[/url] (but even there - to a weaker degree).
In these moments [i]Cantata[/i] [i]really[/i] teeters on the verge of turning into a wargame. 
Or perhaps just turns - into a light one.

I can understand how all this granularity can appear petty and insulting to a refined [i]Command and Conquer 4[/i] veteran. 
But I find it incredible.






Now, to address a few commonly vocalised criticisms.

[b]'AI is almost entirely defensive'[/b]
Yeah, but [spoiler][strike]so is your mom  [/strike] [/spoiler] find me a mainstream granular tile-based turn-based strategy game where it isn't and where AI's 'offensives' and 'counteroffensives' aren't scripted events upon crossing a metaphorical linedef. 
That's not to say they don't exist.
That's to say they're rare beasts.

[b]'Logistics are too finicky'[/b]
Yeah, but [spoiler][strike]_____gotcha_____ [/strike] [/spoiler] that's the beauty of it, man! 
It is truly exciting to both supply and fight at the same time - a completely unique dynamic.

[b]Enemies attack from beyond the fog of war[/b]
Hm... Maybe, I don't know...
Don't stand next to it?
Ever heard of reconnaissance?
Do you stand next to the edge of the screen in beat-em-ups too? [spoiler](ah, who am I kidding)[/spoiler]

[b]'The enemy doesn't get to worry about logistics - they get resupplied each turn for free and out of thin air'[/b]
That [i]is[/i] a fair criticism. It removes an entire dynamic where you could cut enemy supply lines and win by exhaustion.
But it would also be a living hell to write the AI for and to balance.
I regret how it is, but understand the reasoning behind that decision.

[b]'The turn limit kills any incentive towards experimentation'[/b]
On the contrary, turn limit (added post-launch, hurting even more sensibilities - and I have no idea why it wasn't there to begin with) kicks you off your normally resource-hoarding snowballing-inclined butt and gets you moving.
Again, wargame-like.
And the turn limit can (and should) be expanded by discovering new things on the map and doing side objectives. All maps are hand-made and hand-scripted.
 
[b]The developers did a terrible job communicating the game mechanics[/b]
They 100% did, and it's probably what sank the game.
You made a one-of-a-kind game with almost completely unorthodox mechanics, and apart from a single-faction tutorial, all you put out is... 
Detailed pre-release community posts?
You should have taken the [i]Dead Space[/i] 'cut off their limbs' approach, signposting every single minute mechanical detail multiple times over and impressing your vision upon the  player.




So the release failed and the  studio failed, and... Well.

But [i]Cantata[/i] is still here, and still has the capacity to become the cult classic it has all the chops to be.

As far as I'm concerned, there's no stopping [i]Cantata[/i].
